title: Explain Spark execution modes — Cluster mode (driver runs on a worker node, production standard), Client mode (driver on submitter machine, interactive/notebook use), Local mode (single JVM, testing/debugging) — and when to use each.
shortTitle: Spark execution modes — cluster, client, local

s1_definition.profdef: Spark runs in one of three deployment modes that differ in where the Driver process lives. In cluster mode the Driver runs on a worker node inside the cluster, managed by the Cluster Manager, which is the production standard because the job survives independently of the submitting machine. In client mode the Driver runs on the machine that submitted the job, which is convenient for interactive and notebook use because output streams back to the user. In local mode the entire application, Driver and executors, runs inside a single JVM on one machine using threads, which is ideal for development, testing, and debugging.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of launching a reporting project at the National Bank of India. Cluster mode is like sending the project manager to sit permanently inside the data center with the clerks, so even if your laptop is switched off the project keeps running — this is how real production jobs run. Client mode is like the manager staying at their own desk in the branch and phoning instructions to the data center, so they see every update live, which is perfect while exploring data in a notebook, but if their desk shuts down the project dies. Local mode is like doing a tiny pilot entirely at your own desk with no data center at all — quick to try ideas and debug before the real run.
s1_definition.oneliner: Cluster mode puts the Driver inside the cluster for robust production runs, client mode keeps it on your machine for interactive work, and local mode runs everything in one JVM for development and testing.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spark runs in one of three deployment modes that differ in where the Driver process lives. In cluster mode the Driver runs on a worker node inside the cluster, managed by the Cluster Manager, which is the production standard because the job survives independently of the submitting machine. In client mode the Driver runs on the machine that submitted the job, which is convenient for interactive and notebook use because output streams back to the user. In local mode the entire application, Driver and executors, runs inside a single JVM on one machine using threads, which is ideal for development, testing, and debugging.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of launching a reporting project at the National Bank of India. Cluster mode is like sending the project manager to sit permanently inside the data center with the clerks, so even if your laptop is switched off the project keeps running — this is how real production jobs run. Client mode is like the manager staying at their own desk in the branch and phoning instructions to the data center, so they see every update live, which is perfect while exploring data in a notebook, but if their desk shuts down the project dies. Local mode is like doing a tiny pilot entirely at your own desk with no data center at all — quick to try ideas and debug before the real run.

**One line to remember:** Cluster mode puts the Driver inside the cluster for robust production runs, client mode keeps it on your machine for interactive work, and local mode runs everything in one JVM for development and testing.

sections.s2_technical:
The single thing that distinguishes these modes is the location of the Driver, and that location has real consequences for reliability, latency, and resource usage. In cluster mode, you submit the application and the Cluster Manager launches the Driver on one of the worker nodes, then launches the executors around it. Because the Driver lives inside the cluster, the submitting machine can disconnect or shut down and the job continues unaffected. The Driver is also close to the executors on the cluster network, which reduces the latency of scheduling and of collecting results. This is the production standard for long-running batch jobs and scheduled pipelines, where robustness matters more than seeing live output.

In client mode, the Driver runs on the machine that issued the submit command, while the executors still run on the cluster. This is what you get in a notebook or a spark-shell session: every line you run returns output directly to your terminal because the Driver is right there with you. The trade-offs are that the submitting machine must stay up and connected for the whole job, it must have enough memory to be the Driver, and there is extra network latency between your machine and the cluster. Client mode is ideal for interactive exploration, ad hoc analysis, and development, and it is the default for spark-shell and most notebooks.

Local mode runs the whole application — Driver and executors together — in a single JVM on one machine, using threads to simulate parallelism. You choose how many threads with a master setting like local for one thread, local with a number for that many threads, or local with a star for all available cores. There is no cluster and no Cluster Manager involved. This is perfect for unit tests, continuous integration pipelines, and debugging logic on a small sample before deploying to a real cluster, because it is fast to start and easy to attach a debugger to.

A senior nuance is choosing correctly in practice. Use cluster mode for scheduled production jobs so a failed or disconnected launcher never kills a running pipeline, and so the Driver gets proper resources on the cluster. Use client mode for interactive and notebook work where immediate feedback matters, but be aware the launcher is now a single point of failure for the job. Use local mode strictly for development, testing, and small data, never for real workloads, because a single JVM cannot provide real distributed scale or fault tolerance. In the bank, our Airflow-scheduled nightly jobs always ran in cluster mode, data scientists explored in client-mode notebooks, and our test suite ran Spark in local mode so it needed no cluster at all.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A scheduled nightly report must keep running even if the machine that launched it is switched off. This is exactly cluster mode, with the Driver inside the cluster.

Problem 2 — A data scientist exploring transactions in a notebook needs to see each result immediately. This is exactly client mode, with the Driver on their machine.

Problem 3 — The engineering team must unit-test the report logic quickly with no cluster. This is exactly local mode, everything in one JVM.

The mini-project models the three modes in Java. A `DeploymentMode` enum captures CLUSTER, CLIENT, and LOCAL. A `SparkLauncher` reports where the Driver runs and whether the job survives if the launcher disconnects, then runs the same small account-totalling computation in each mode. The demo runs Rajesh's and Priya's transactions in all three modes and prints the behavioural differences.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the modes demo
java -cp target/exec-modes-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.modes.ModesDemo

# Reference real submits:
# Cluster mode (production nightly job):
spark-submit --master yarn --deploy-mode cluster --class com.bank.NightlyReportJob report.jar
# Client mode (interactive):
spark-shell --master yarn --deploy-mode client
# Local mode (unit tests):
spark-submit --master "local[*]" --class com.bank.NightlyReportJob report.jar
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transactions — Rajesh Rs.1000, Priya Rs.500, Rajesh Rs.3000. The same computation, totalling per account, runs in all three modes.

Step 1: Cluster mode runs first. The launcher reports that the Driver runs on a worker node inside the cluster and that the job survives if the launcher disconnects, which is why it is the production standard. The computation totals Rajesh to Rs.4000 and Priya to Rs.500.

Step 2: Client mode runs next. The launcher reports that the Driver runs on the submitting machine and warns that the launcher is now a single point of failure for the job, which is acceptable for interactive notebooks where live output matters. The totals are identical.

Step 3: Local mode runs last. The launcher reports that the Driver and executors share one JVM with no cluster, which is ideal for unit tests and debugging small data. The totals are again identical.

Step 4: The key observation is that the computation and its result are the same in every mode; what differs is where the Driver lives and the operational consequences — robustness in cluster mode, interactivity in client mode, and simplicity in local mode.

Step 5: The journey makes concrete that choosing a mode is an operational decision about reliability and feedback, not about the data logic.

Step 6: The final totals in each mode are Rajesh Rs.4000 and Priya Rs.500, confirming identical results across modes.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  CLUSTER MODE (production):
  Launcher ──submit──→ ClusterManager ──launches──→ Driver(on worker) ──→ Executors
      │  (may disconnect)                                 │
      └── job keeps running                             ▼ result to Driver / storage

  CLIENT MODE (interactive):
  Launcher machine [Driver lives here] ──schedules──→ Executors(on cluster)
      │  (must stay up)                                    │
      └── if launcher dies → job dies                    ▼ output streams back live

  LOCAL MODE (test/debug):
  Single JVM: [Driver + Executors as threads]  (no cluster, no ClusterManager)
      └── local[*] → use all cores ; great for unit tests
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Deployment Mode Model ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Strategy (via enum): mode selects driver placement behavior │
  │     WHY: same computation, different operational semantics   │
  │  Enum-as-config: each mode carries its own metadata          │
  │     WHY: self-describing modes, no scattered if-else         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: DeploymentMode describes placement; Launcher runs the job│
  │  O: add a new mode (e.g., k8s-cluster) = new enum constant   │
  │  L: any DeploymentMode works wherever a mode is expected     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │     <<enum>> DeploymentMode  │◀───────│       SparkLauncher       │
  │──────────────────────────────│ uses   │──────────────────────────│
  │ CLUSTER, CLIENT, LOCAL       │        │ + run(mode, txns): Map    │
  │ - driverLocation: String     │        └──────────────────────────┘
  │ - survivesLauncherLoss: bool │
  │ - bestFor: String            │
  │ + driverLocation()           │
  │ + survivesLauncherLoss()     │
  │ + bestFor()                  │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Job vs Launcher ─────────────────────────────

  CLUSTER:  [RUNNING] ──launcher disconnects──→ [STILL_RUNNING]
  CLIENT :  [RUNNING] ──launcher dies──────────→ [KILLED]
  LOCAL  :  [RUNNING] ──JVM exits──────────────→ [KILLED] (expected)

  ── Call Chain ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. ModesDemo.main()
  2.   → for each DeploymentMode:
  3.       → launcher.run(mode, txns)
  4.         → describe driver placement + durability
  5.         → compute totals → {SAV:4000, CUR:500}
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Spark has three deployment modes, and the single thing that distinguishes them is where the Driver process runs, which in turn drives reliability, latency, and how you use the job. In cluster mode the Cluster Manager launches the Driver on a worker node inside the cluster, so the submitting machine can disconnect or shut down and the job keeps running, and the Driver sits on the fast cluster network close to the executors. This is the production standard for scheduled batch jobs and pipelines because robustness is what matters there.

In client mode the Driver runs on the machine that submitted the job while the executors run on the cluster, which is exactly what a notebook or spark-shell gives you: every command returns output live to your terminal because the Driver is right there. The cost is that the submitting machine must stay up and connected for the whole job and becomes a single point of failure, so client mode is for interactive exploration and development rather than durable production runs. Local mode runs the Driver and executors together in a single JVM using threads, with a master like local with a star to use all cores, and it is meant purely for unit tests, continuous integration, and debugging on small data, because one JVM gives you neither distributed scale nor real fault tolerance.

In my project at the National Bank of India we matched each mode to its purpose deliberately. Our Airflow-scheduled nightly reconciliation and reporting jobs always ran in cluster mode so that a flaky launcher or a disconnected laptop could never kill a running pipeline, and so the Driver got proper resources on the cluster. Data scientists explored transaction data in client-mode notebooks where seeing each result immediately was the whole point. And our automated test suite ran Spark in local mode so it needed no cluster at all, which kept continuous integration fast and self-contained. Choosing the mode is an operational decision about reliability and feedback, not about the data logic, which stays identical across all three.
